content: Many women prefer to avoid pharmacological or invasive methods for managing pain during labor, which has led to the growing popularity of complementary approaches such as manual methods. This review focused on evaluating the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of manual techniques, including massage, reflexology, and other related methods, for pain management during labor. The review is an update of a previous analysis first published in 2012. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries up to August 2017. They included randomized controlled trials that compared manual methods with standard care, other non-pharmacological pain management techniques, no treatment, or placebo. The manual methods assessed included massage, warm packs, thermal manual methods, reflexology, chiropractic techniques, osteopathy, musculoskeletal manipulation, deep tissue massage, neuromuscular therapy, shiatsu, tuina, trigger point therapy, myotherapy, and zero balancing. Trials involving hypnosis, aromatherapy, acupuncture, and acupressure were excluded, as these are covered in other reviews. The review included 14 trials, with 10 trials (involving 1055 women) contributing data to the meta-analysis. Four additional trials met the inclusion criteria but did not provide usable data. Over half of the trials demonstrated a low risk of bias for random sequence generation and attrition bias, but most had a high risk of performance and detection bias, with unclear reporting bias. Notably, no trials specifically examined the effectiveness of reflexology. Massage Evidence of low quality suggested that massage reduced pain intensity during the first stage of labor compared to usual care, as measured by self-reported pain scales (SMD −0.81, 95% CI −1.06 to −0.56; six trials, 362 women). During the second and third stages of labor, two trials indicated a reduction in pain scores favoring massage (SMD −0.98, 95% CI −2.23 to 0.26, 124 women; and SMD −1.03, 95% CI −2.17 to 0.11, 122 women). Very low-quality evidence showed no clear benefit of massage over usual care for the duration of labor (MD 20.64 minutes, 95% CI −58.24 to 99.52; six trials, 514 women) or the use of pharmacological pain relief (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.74; four trials, 105 women). Similarly, very low-quality evidence showed no clear benefit of massage for reducing assisted vaginal births (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.13; four trials, 368 women) or cesarean sections (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.09; six trials, 514 women). One trial reported reduced anxiety during the first stage of labor for women receiving massage (MD −16.27, 95% CI −27.03 to −5.51; 60 women). Another trial found that massage increased women’s sense of control during labor (MD 14.05, 95% CI 3.77 to 24.33; 124 women, low-quality evidence). Two trials assessing satisfaction with the childbirth experience found higher satisfaction levels with massage, though the evidence quality was low in one study and very low in the other. Warm Packs Very low-quality evidence suggested that warm packs reduced pain intensity during the first stage of labor (SMD −0.59, 95% CI −1.18 to −0.00; three trials, 191 women) and the second stage of labor (SMD −1.49, 95% CI −2.85 to −0.13; two trials, 128 women). Warm packs were associated with a reduced duration of labor (MD −66.15 minutes, 95% CI −91.83 to −40.47; two trials, 128 women), though the evidence was of very low quality. Thermal Manual Methods One trial evaluated thermal manual methods and found very low-quality evidence of reduced pain intensity during the first stage of labor (MD −1.44, 95% CI −2.24 to −0.65; one trial, 96 women). The same trial reported a reduction in labor duration (MD −78.24 minutes, 95% CI −118.75 to −37.73; one trial, 96 women, very low-quality evidence). There was no clear difference in the rate of assisted vaginal births (very low-quality evidence). Results were similar for cold packs and intermittent hot and cold packs compared to usual care, with no significant differences in pain intensity, labor duration, or assisted vaginal births. Music Comparison One trial compared manual methods with music and found very low-quality evidence that massage reduced pain intensity during labor (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.89; 101 women). There was no evidence of benefit for reduced use of pharmacological pain relief (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.08; very low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions Massage, warm packs, and thermal manual methods may help reduce pain, shorten labor duration, and improve women’s sense of control and emotional experience during labor. However, the quality of evidence ranges from low to very low, and few trials reported on key outcomes such as safety. Further research is needed to better understand the effectiveness and safety of these manual methods for pain management during labor.
